title: A force-to-acceleration ratio needs two frame labels
question: Why are there two transverse coefficients?
recap: Einstein’s transverse mass, m times gamma squared, divides the force measured in the electron’s momentary rest frame by the acceleration measured in the laboratory. Measure both in the laboratory and the ratio is m times gamma. The two numbers answer two different questions; the electron has one mass m.
premises: In its momentary rest frame the electron obeys ordinary mechanics for slow motion.
Every force and every acceleration is labelled with the frame it is measured in.
limitations: The two masses are ratios of force to acceleration under stated conventions; the electron’s own mass does not change with the observer’s speed.
The electron is treated as a point driven slowly, without the effects of its own radiation or field.

overview.text: Einstein’s transverse mass, \(m\gamma^2\), divides the force measured in the electron’s momentary rest frame by the acceleration measured in the laboratory. Measure both in the laboratory and the ratio is \(m\gamma\). The two numbers answer two different questions; the electron has one mass \(m\).

full.spoken: Longitudinal laboratory force over acceleration is m gamma cubed. Rest-frame transverse force over laboratory acceleration is m gamma squared. Laboratory transverse force over laboratory acceleration is m gamma.

full.text: For an electron moving along \(x\), a force across the motion is \(\gamma\) times larger in the electron’s momentary rest frame than in the laboratory. Einstein divides the rest-frame force by the laboratory acceleration and gets \(m\gamma^2\). Dividing the laboratory force by the same acceleration gives \(m\gamma\).

At \(0.6c\), \(\gamma = 1.25\). The longitudinal mass is \(m\gamma^3 = 1.953125\,m\), Einstein’s transverse mass is \(m\gamma^2 = 1.5625\,m\), and the all-laboratory transverse ratio is \(m\gamma = 1.25\,m\). The electron-dynamics laboratory shows each number with the frames it uses, and leaves Einstein’s result as he printed it.

full.returnCaption: Return to why there are two transverse coefficients.

steps.text: Letters: in §10 the paper's electron is a point particle of charge ε and mass μ, where μ is its mass while it moves slowly; X, Y, Z are the electric force and M, N magnetic components, in Gaussian units; β is the modern γ and V the speed of light. This explanation writes m for μ, and F with a frame label for each force.

items: The only assumption about the law of motion: when the electron is at rest at some moment, in the next instant it moves by \(\mu\frac{d^2x}{dt^2}=ε X\), and likewise for y and z, ordinary mechanics for slow motion.

Now let the electron have speed v along x at the moment t = 0, at the origin of K. It is then at rest in the system k moving at v, so in k, for small times, \(\mu\frac{d^2ξ}{d\tau^2}=ε X'\) and likewise for η and ζ.

Transform back to K with §3 and §6, using \(X'=X\), \(Y'=\beta(Y-\frac{v}{V}N)\), \(Z'=\beta(Z+\frac{v}{V}M)\). The paper's equations (A): \(\frac{d^2x}{dt^2}=\frac{ε}{\mu}\frac{1}{\beta^3}X\), \(\frac{d^2y}{dt^2}=\frac{ε}{\mu}\frac{1}{\beta}(Y-\frac{v}{V}N)\), and the same for z.
Rewrite them as the paper does: \(\mu\beta^3\frac{d^2x}{dt^2}=ε X=ε X'\) and \(\mu\beta^2\frac{d^2y}{dt^2}=ε\beta(Y-\frac{v}{V}N)=ε Y'\).
Read \(εX'\), \(εY'\), \(εZ'\) as the force on the electron measured in a system moving with it at that moment; the paper says it could be measured with a spring balance at rest in that system.

Keep mass times acceleration equal to force, with that force and with accelerations measured in K. Then the ratio of force to acceleration is \(\mu\beta^3\) along the motion and \(\mu\beta^2\) across it: the paper's longitudinal mass \(\mu/(\sqrt{1-(v/V)^2})^3\) and transverse mass \(\mu/(1-(v/V)^2)\).
Measure the transverse force in K as well: it is smaller than the co-moving force by the factor β, so that ratio is \(m\gamma\). The three ratios are below.

steps.spoken: Longitudinal laboratory force over acceleration is m gamma cubed. Rest-frame transverse force over laboratory acceleration is m gamma squared. Laboratory transverse force over laboratory acceleration is m gamma.

items: Worked at 0.6c, γ = 1.25: longitudinal 1.953125 m, Einstein's transverse 1.5625 m, and the all-laboratory transverse ratio 1.25 m.

The paper's own warning, kept with its result: with other definitions of force and of acceleration, other numbers for these masses would be obtained, so theories of the electron's motion must be compared with great care.

The transverse mass \(m\gamma^2\) is Einstein's, under his convention: force measured in the co-moving system, acceleration in K. The later habit of defining force as the rate of change of momentum gives \(m\gamma\) for the same transverse case; it is a different convention, and it does not correct his result.
The paper adds that these results hold for any ponderable material point too, since a vanishingly small charge turns it into an electron in its sense.
The electron's mass m is one number; each ratio depends on the direction of the force and on the frames used, and m does not.

steps.returnCaption: Return to why there are two transverse coefficients.

margin.text: Einstein himself warns that other definitions of force and acceleration would give other values for these masses. The modern habit of defining force as the rate of change of momentum gives \(m\gamma\) for the transverse ratio. It is a later convention, and this edition does not substitute it for his printed result.
